content: Polycomb complex protein BMI-1, also referred to as polycomb group RING finger protein 4 (PCGF4) or RING finger protein 51 (RNF51), is a protein encoded by the BMI1 gene in humans. The BMI1 gene is also known as the B cell-specific Moloney murine leukemia virus integration site 1. BMI1 functions as a polycomb ring finger oncogene. Function BMI1 has been identified as an oncogene due to its role in regulating the cell cycle inhibitor genes p16 and p19. In mice, the absence of BMI1 (via knockout models) leads to significant defects in hematopoiesis, skeletal patterning, neurological functions, and cerebellar development. Recent studies have demonstrated that BMI1 is rapidly recruited to sites of DNA damage and remains active for over 8 hours. Loss of BMI1 results in increased sensitivity to radiation and impaired repair of DNA double-strand breaks through homologous recombination. BMI1 is essential for the efficient self-renewal of adult hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and neural stem cells in both the peripheral and central nervous systems. However, it plays a less critical role in the generation of differentiated progeny. Given its broad tissue distribution and the numerous phenotypic changes observed in BMI1 knockout mice, it is hypothesized that BMI1 may regulate the self-renewal of other types of somatic stem cells. Additionally, BMI1 is believed to inhibit neuronal aging by suppressing the activity of p53. BMI1 expression interacts with several key signaling pathways, including Wnt, Akt, Notch, Hedgehog, and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) pathways. In the context of Ewing sarcoma family of tumors (ESFT), silencing the BMI1 gene significantly impacts the Notch and Wnt signaling pathways, which are critical for the formation and progression of these tumors. BMI1 has also been shown to mediate the effects of the Hedgehog signaling pathway on mammary stem cell proliferation. BMI1 regulates multiple downstream genes and factors. It represses the expression of p19Arf and p16Ink4a. Neural stem cells and hematopoietic stem cells lacking BMI1 (BMI1-/-) exhibit elevated levels of p19Arf and p16Ink4a, which leads to reduced proliferation rates. Furthermore, BMI1 is a key regulator of Th2 cell differentiation and development, as it stabilizes GATA transcription factors. Structure The BMI1 gene spans 10.04 kilobases and contains 10 exons. It is highly conserved across species. In humans, the BMI1 gene is located on chromosome 10 at position 10p11.23. The BMI1 protein consists of 326 amino acids and has a molecular weight of approximately 36,949 Daltons. Structurally, BMI1 contains a RING finger domain at its N-terminus and a central helix-turn-helix domain. The RING finger domain is a cysteine-rich domain involved in zinc binding and plays a critical role in the ubiquitination process. The interaction between BMI1 and Ring1B significantly enhances E3 ubiquitin ligase activity. Both the RING domain and the extended N-terminal tail are essential for the interaction between BMI1 and Ring1B. Clinical Significance Overexpression of BMI1 has been implicated in the development of various cancers, including bladder, skin, prostate, breast, ovarian, colorectal, and hematological malignancies. Its amplification and overexpression are particularly prominent in mantle cell lymphomas. Inhibiting BMI1 has been shown to suppress the proliferation of glioblastoma multiforme, chemoresistant ovarian cancer, and cancers of the prostate, pancreas, and skin. In colorectal cancer, BMI1 inhibition reduces the self-renewal capacity of cancer stem cells. In mouse xenograft models, colon cancer stem cells were effectively eliminated by targeting the BMI1 gene, suggesting a potential therapeutic approach for colorectal cancer. A study conducted by Canadian researchers suggests that the loss of BMI1 gene expression in human neurons may contribute directly to the development of Alzheimer’s disease. Interactions BMI1 has been shown to interact with the following proteins: PHC1, PHC2, RING1, and ZBTB16.
